1. The Blanket of Air
2. Weather and Climate
3. The Blanket Grows Thicker
4. What We Are Already Seeing
5. Why It Matters Here
6. The Good News
7. Your Part in It

climate: the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years
weather: what the sky is doing on a particular day
climate change: the slow warming of the whole planet caused by people
greenhouse gas: a gas that traps extra heat in the air
renewable energy: clean power from sun, wind or water that will not run out
drought: a long period with little or no rain

Our Earth is wrapped in a thin layer of air, and that air does something wonderful. It works like a blanket, holding in just enough of the Sun's warmth to keep the whole planet at a comfortable temperature. Without this blanket of air, the Earth would be a frozen, lifeless ball. It is the reason our world is warm enough for life.

image.note: The Earth wrapped in a soft glowing layer of air, keeping in gentle warmth; cosy, protective

pages.text: This warming is completely natural and entirely good. For thousands of years, the blanket held the Earth at just the right warmth, and life flourished. The trouble begins only when the blanket grows too thick, and holds in more heat than it should. To understand how that happens, we first need to understand the difference between weather and climate.

image.note: A balanced, healthy Earth basking in just-right warmth; the natural greenhouse working well

pages.text: Weather is what is happening in the sky today: sunny, rainy, windy, hot or cool. It changes from hour to hour and day to day. Climate is different. Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a place over many, many years. Weather is your mood today. Climate is your character over a lifetime.

image.note: Split image: a single rainy day (weather) beside a long calendar of typical seasons (climate)

pages.text: So when scientists say the climate is changing, they do not mean it rained yesterday. They mean the whole long pattern is shifting: the Earth's usual temperature is slowly, steadily rising, year after year, all around the world. This slow warming of the entire planet is what we call climate change, and it is caused by that blanket of air growing too thick.

image.note: A long graph of the Earth's average temperature slowly rising over many years; clear, calm

pages.text: What is thickening the blanket? Certain gases in the air, especially one released when we burn coal, oil and petrol, trap extra heat. For two hundred years, humans have burned more and more of these fuels, to power factories, cars and homes. Each year, we add more of these heat-trapping gases, and the blanket holds in a little more warmth.

image.note: Chimneys and traffic releasing gas that thickens the air-blanket around the Earth; cause shown clearly

pages.text: Trees would normally help, for growing plants soak up that very gas and clean the air. But at the same time, great forests are being cut down across the world. So we are adding more heat-trapping gas while removing the very things that could remove it. The blanket thickens, and the Earth grows slowly warmer.

image.note: A shrinking forest beside rising smoke; the two problems together; sobering but not terrifying

pages.text: This is not a worry only for the future. It is already happening. The great sheets of ice at the frozen ends of the Earth are melting, which makes the seas slowly rise. Weather is growing wilder in many places, with fiercer storms, longer droughts and heavier floods than before. The warming blanket is already changing our world.

image.note: Melting polar ice and a rising sea; a distant flooded coast; real but not showing people harmed

pages.text: None of this means the world is ending. It means the world is changing, faster than it naturally would, because of what people have done. And here is the most important truth in this whole book: because the problem was caused by people, it can also be solved by people. That is not a small hope. It is everything.

image.note: A hand reaching to steady a tilting Earth; the idea that we can act; empowering, calm

pages.text: Africa has done less than almost anywhere to cause this problem, for it has burned far less fuel than the wealthy nations. Yet it often feels the effects strongly. In parts of Nigeria and its neighbours, farmers face harder droughts and less reliable rains, which makes it tougher to grow the food everyone needs.

image.note: A Nigerian farmer looking at a dry field and a clouded sky; concerned but dignified; local, real

pages.text: This makes it only fair that the countries that caused most of the problem should do most to fix it, and should help others too. But everyone, everywhere, has a part to play. And Africa, blessed with some of the strongest sunshine on Earth, is in a wonderful position to lead the way with clean, sunlit power.

image.note: Solar panels gleaming under a bright African sun; opportunity and fairness together; hopeful

pages.text: Now for the good news, and there is a great deal of it. We already know how to fix this. We can make our power from the sun, the wind and the rivers, which give off no heat-trapping gas at all. Around the world, clean energy is spreading fast and growing cheaper every year. The tools to heal the blanket already exist.

image.note: A bright scene of solar panels, wind turbines and a green city; clean energy thriving; optimistic

pages.text: We can plant trees to soak up the gas and cool the land. We can build things to last instead of throwing them away. We can waste less power and less water. None of this is beyond us. It simply takes people who understand the problem and decide to act. And more and more people, especially the young, are deciding exactly that.

image.note: Children and adults planting trees together, a greener estate rising; community action; warm

pages.text: You did not cause this problem. It was handed to you, which is not fair. But you have something powerful: you are young, and the future is longer for you than for anyone. The choices your generation makes will shape the climate of the whole century to come. That is a heavy load, but it is also a mighty chance to do good.

image.note: A group of children looking out over a landscape, determined and hopeful; the future in their hands

pages.text: So do not be frightened. Be informed, and be ready. Learn how the world works, waste less, plant what you can, and speak up for a cleaner future. The Earth has kept us warm and safe for a very long time. Now, in your lifetime, it needs its people to look after it in return. It is the only home we have, and it is worth every effort.

image.note: A child gently holding a small healthy globe, looking at the reader; caretaking, closing, hopeful
